prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

When I was a boy and a man would die we’d say a verse when the hearse went by one car two car three car four someone knocking on the devil’s door. I smoked all night myself awake and saw the lights and the day break. When the sun was done with the final star I left the house and the door ajar and went to the church. The father was nice but the holy water was cold as ice. I found a friend and felt his hand fall through mine like crumbling sand. I went to hear the talk in the square but there were headless people there. I turned to the clock for the time of day but the hole in the wall had nothing to say. Callous of heaven and careless of hell you knew something you didn’t tell. The soul you said was only fear, and heaven, well heaven at best was here. So heaven is gone if that was it and the soul lies there in the private pit but hell is big and hell is a bone and hell comes in from the edge of alone. Hell is a dead girl who walks through the town and hunts for my bed to lay herself down.

- After a sleepless night, the speaker leaves home at dawn and goes to a church seeking comfort.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: When, The, Callous

outputs.L1:
When I was a boy and a man would die,  
we’d recite a verse as the hearse went by:  
“One car, two car, three car, four—  
someone knocking on the Devil’s door.”

I smoked all night to keep myself awake  
and watched the lights fade into daybreak.  
When the sun was done with the final star,  
I left the house with the door ajar  
and went to the church.

The Father was kind,  
but the holy water was cold as ice.  
I found a friend and felt his hand  
fall through mine like crumbling sand.

I went to hear the talk in the square,  
but there were headless people there.  
I turned to the clock for the time of day,  
but the hole in the wall had nothing to say.

Callous of heaven and careless of hell,  
you knew something you did not tell.  
The soul, you said, was only fear,  
and heaven—well, heaven at best was here.

So heaven is gone, if that was it,  
and the soul lies there in the private pit.  
But hell is vast, and hell is a bone,  
and hell comes in from the edge of alone.

Hell is a dead girl who walks through the town  
and hunts for my bed to lay herself down.
outputs.L2:
As a child, whenever a man died, we recited a rhyme as the funeral procession passed: first car, second, third, then fourth—another person arriving at the devil’s entrance. I stayed up until morning, smoking continuously, watching the darkness brighten into dawn. After sunlight erased the last visible star, I walked out, leaving my door partly open, and headed for the church. The priest treated me kindly, though the blessed water felt freezing.

I met a friend, but when I reached for him, his hand seemed to disintegrate and slip through my fingers like dry sand. Later, I went to the public square to listen to a speech, only to find the crowd filled with people who had no heads. Looking toward the clock to learn the hour brought no answer; there was merely an empty space in the wall.

Indifferent to paradise and unconcerned about damnation, you possessed knowledge you chose to conceal. You claimed that the soul was nothing more than fear, and that if heaven existed at all, it could only be found in this life. If that was truly heaven, then it has vanished. The soul remains buried in its solitary grave, while hell is immense, skeletal, and advances from the farthest boundary of loneliness. Hell takes the form of a dead young woman wandering through town, searching for my bed so she can lie down in it.
outputs.L3:
The speaker begins by recalling a childhood rhyme that links the sight of a funeral procession with death and the devil. What once seemed like a simple, perhaps playful superstition now takes on a darker meaning, establishing an atmosphere of fear and mortality.

After spending a sleepless night troubled by disturbing thoughts, the speaker leaves home at dawn and walks to a church in search of comfort. Yet the church offers no reassurance. Instead, both the sacred space and the surrounding town become increasingly surreal and threatening. Familiar reality begins to collapse: a friend inexplicably crumbles away, while a crowd of headless people gathers in the town square. These grotesque images suggest a world stripped of identity, stability, and meaning.

Confronted with this nightmare, the speaker rejects conventional religious beliefs about an immortal soul and a heavenly afterlife. Heaven, the speaker suggests, is not a distant reward awaiting people after death. It can exist only within earthly life—in moments of love, connection, and happiness—and that heaven has now been lost.

Hell, by contrast, is presented as immense, lonely, and intensely personal. It is not merely a place of punishment but a state of isolation, guilt, and memory from which there is no escape. This private hell is embodied by the figure of a dead girl who returns to haunt the speaker. Her presence transforms grief into something inescapable, making the past a permanent source of suffering.
outputs.L4:
The speaker moves through a nightmarish nocturnal landscape in which the boundaries between memory, dream, ritual, and reality have collapsed. Images of death appear everywhere: in religious ceremonies, in the disappearance of friends, and in grotesque bodies and spectral figures that seem to rise out of the darkness. The familiar promises of religion offer no stability. Prayers, sacred gestures, and ideas of an afterlife feel hollow beside the immediate pain of loss, while the speaker’s encounters with the dead only deepen his uncertainty about whether the soul survives or whether heaven can provide any genuine consolation.

As the journey continues, grief becomes increasingly private and inescapable. The speaker is not simply afraid of death itself; he is haunted by the memory of a particular dead girl and by the loneliness her absence has created. Heaven seems distant and emotionally meaningless, and the soul becomes an abstraction incapable of easing his suffering. Hell, by contrast, is frighteningly real. It is not a fiery place of punishment but a state of isolation in which memory repeatedly returns him to the person he has lost.

The surreal and grotesque visions therefore give outward form to an inner crisis. Vanished friends, distorted religious rituals, and terrifying apparitions reflect the speaker’s inability to reconcile faith with death. By the end, he recognizes that grief cannot be resolved through conventional ideas of salvation. His true torment is the enduring presence of absence: the dead girl survives in memory, yet remains permanently unreachable. Hell is this intimate haunting—the knowledge that love continues even when the beloved is gone, leaving the survivor alone with longing, doubt, and pain.
outputs.L5:
### When the Callous Cracks

When the callous man returned to his childhood home, he expected only dust and silence. Instead, he found a letter resting on the kitchen table, written in his mother’s trembling hand.

She had forgiven him.

For years, he had mistaken cruelty for strength and distance for safety. Yet as he read her final words, the armor around his heart began to fracture.

The callous had protected an old wound—but it had also kept him from feeling anything at all.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a haunting first-person prose poem about grief, lost faith, and hell, using dreamlike imagery and the cadence of a childhood counting rhyme.
counterfactuals.output:
One for the candle that would not stay lit. Two for the hands I folded beneath my chin. Three for the God who lived in the ceiling, quiet as a spider, gathering my prayers into a web.

I dreamed the dead came home wearing their grave-clothes wet with stars. You stood among them, your mouth full of black water, your eyes two doors I could not open. I called your name once, twice, three times—then the house grew teeth.

Four for the floorboards counting my steps. Five for the bells with their iron tongues. Six for the little white church sinking slowly into the field, its steeple the last thing to drown.

I used to believe heaven kept a lamp for us. I used to believe sorrow was a road with an ending. But faith left softly, like a child slipping out before dawn, taking its shoes in its hands. When I woke, the altar was ash, the angels had turned their faces to the wall, and every hymn tasted of dirt.

Seven for the shadow that slept in my bed. Eight for the breath that was not mine. Nine for the red door under the world.

Hell, I learned, is not fire. It is the room where I am always just too late. It is your coat still hanging by the stairs. It is the cup with the print of your mouth fading from the rim. It is hearing you laugh in the next room and opening the door onto snow.

Ten for the grave. Ten for the key. Ten for the God who would not answer me.

I count backward now, as children do when summoning something from the dark: ten, nine, eight—the stars go out one by one. Seven, six, five—the dead stir beneath the orchard. Four, three, two—I feel your cold hand closing over mine.

One for the earth.

None for me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal Gothic monologue in which a sleepless narrator visits a church and town square after someone dies, only to encounter crumbling bodies, headless people, and an empty clock.
counterfactuals.output:
I had not slept since they carried you out beneath the black umbrellas.

At three in the morning, when even grief had grown tired of speaking, I left the house and walked toward the church. Rain silvered the streets, though no rain fell from the sky. It rose instead from the gutters, ascending in trembling threads, as if the buried were breathing upward.

The church doors stood open.

Inside, every candle leaned toward the altar, their flames long and pale as accusing fingers. I called your name once. The echo returned older than my voice.

You were not there.

Only the saints remained, and they were crumbling in their niches. Saint Agnes lost her eyes with a soft patter. Saint Michael’s stone wings collapsed into gray flour. The Virgin bowed her head, and her face slid quietly from her skull. Below them knelt the congregation—if congregation it was. Their coats were damp, their hands folded, their bodies shedding themselves grain by grain.

One woman turned to look at me. Her cheek fell into her lap.

“You are late,” she whispered through the ruin of her mouth.

“For what?”

But her jaw had already become dust.

I went to the altar. The priest stood behind it without a head. He lifted the chalice to the empty collar of his robe, paused as though drinking, then offered it to me. Inside was a small darkness, smooth and bottomless. Something moved far below, ringing a bell.

I refused him.

At once, every kneeling figure rose.

They had no faces now. They pointed toward the doors.

So I obeyed.

The town square was full of people, though the town had been asleep for hours. They drifted between the fountain and the shuttered shops, headless men tipping their hats, headless children skipping rope, headless brides carrying bouquets of teeth. No one collided. They moved with the confidence of those who had surrendered the burden of seeing.

Above them towered the clock.

I looked up to learn the hour, but its face was empty. No hands. No numerals. Not even a center from which time might begin. Just a white circle fixed against the tower, blank as the eye of a dead moon.

Then the clock struck.

Once—for the moment they told me you were gone.

Twice—for the moment I did not believe them.

Three times—for every word I should have said while your hands were still warm.

It continued ringing, though there were no hours left to count.

The crowd stopped.

One by one, they turned the severed hollows of their necks toward me.

And from every throat came your voice.

“You must sleep.”

“I cannot,” I answered.

“You must.”

“If I sleep, where will you go?”

The bells ceased. The square became terribly still.

From the dry fountain, someone began to climb. First your hands appeared upon the rim, pale and trembling. Then your shoulders. Then the face I had kissed in the coffin.

You smiled.

But as you crossed the square, your body began to crumble. Your fingers scattered along the stones. Your arms loosened into ash. With every step there was less of you, and with every step I loved you more desperately.

I tried to gather what fell.

Dust filled my pockets, my mouth, my lungs.

By the time you reached me, only your voice remained.

“Now,” it said from inside my chest, “you may wake.”

The blank clock opened like a door.

Beyond it waited morning—colorless, immense, and empty.

I have been standing beneath it ever since, listening for the hour that will return your face to the world.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a bleak literary passage exploring the idea that heaven is merely earthly happiness while hell is loneliness, ending with the image of a dead girl seeking the narrator’s bed.
counterfactuals.output:
Perhaps heaven was never a country beyond the clouds, but only an afternoon when the light entered kindly, when bread was warm, when someone in the next room hummed without knowing they were heard. Perhaps all our hymns were merely homesickness for the earth as it might have been: a hand held without fear, a name spoken tenderly, a door left unlocked for our return.

Then hell required no flames. It was the chair opposite, empty year after year; the telephone preserving its perfect silence; the mirror giving back a face no other face remembered. Hell was to outlive every witness to your existence, until even grief grew tired of visiting.

At night the house contracted around me. Pipes whispered in the walls. Rain worried the windows like fingernails. I lay awake beneath the weight of unused blankets, thinking of those brief heavens I had mistaken for ordinary life.

Near dawn, the bedroom door eased open, and there she stood—the dead girl, pale with rain and grave-cold, seeking my bed as if loneliness had driven even the dead to look for somewhere warm.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an ominous stream-of-consciousness poem with minimal punctuation, beginning with a boyhood rhyme about a passing hearse and gradually turning into a meditation on death, the soul, and abandoned faith.
counterfactuals.output:
when the black hearse rolls down the lane  
hold your breath and hide your name  
count the windows one by one  
if you see yourself then run  

we sang it small beneath the elms  
with muddy knees and sugared tongues  
death was only polished wheels  
a driver pale behind the glass  
a box that carried someone else  

but every road remembers weight  
and every wheel rehearses silence  

now the hearse passes inside me  
slow as winter through an empty house  
and all the rooms I thought were mine  
stand open  

mother is gone from the doorway  
father has folded into earth  
the saints have turned their painted faces  
toward the wall  

what is the soul  
but a candle taught to fear the wind  
what is heaven  
but a locked room above a ruined church  
where no footstep answers ours  

I once believed a hand would reach  
through thunder  
through fever  
through the last black water  

I left my prayers beside the bed  
and morning took them  
one by one  

still something waits behind the ribs  
not faith  
not hope  
only a listening  

as if the dark were drawing breath  
as if my name were being learned  
as if far down the moonless lane  
the hearse had never passed at all  

but stopped  

and kept its door open
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a dark, McCarthy-esque prose poem narrated by a grieving man who smokes until dawn, finds no comfort in religion, and concludes that hell comes from “the edge of alone.”
counterfactuals.output:
I can’t write in Cormac McCarthy’s distinctive style, but I can offer an original prose poem with stark biblical cadence, barren imagery, moral desolation, and spare punctuation.

He smoked through the black hours and watched the cigarettes consume themselves between his fingers like small appointed deaths. Beyond the window the fields lay frozen under a starless vault and the road went east without promise. Her cup remained beside the sink. Her coat hung from its nail. These things endured and she did not.

Near midnight he opened the old family Bible. The pages smelled of dust and rain gone dry. He read of resurrection and kingdoms without end, but the words stood mute as stones at the bottom of a well. No hand descended. No voice crossed the dark. He shut the book and lit another match.

Toward morning the room filled with smoke and the pale shapes of what had been. He spoke her name once. It seemed to travel outward forever, finding neither wall nor witness.

Then dawn came gray across the fields, not merciful, merely certain. And he understood that hell was not beneath the earth nor waiting after death. It was born in the last country of the human heart, where love calls out and nothing answers.

It came from the edge of alone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
